title: The storehouse at Sultanpur
hookLine: weighing out grain as a storekeeper, he reaches thirteen, tera, which also means yours, and keeps saying it

cards: Sultanpur. A young man stands in the government storehouse, in charge of the governor's grain. It comes in as taxes and goes out as wages and supplies, and the governor, Daulat Khan Lodi, wants someone honest running it.
His sister's husband, Jai Ram, found him the job: steady, respectable, the kind his father hoped for. Tradition says Nanak is good at it, and honest.
He has a family of his own now, and for a while it looks as if Mehta Kalu's son has settled down. Then comes the day he starts counting.

teach.b: The storehouse was the modikhana, and a storekeeper measured grain the old way: a scoop, a scale, counting aloud as each measure went into a customer's bag. Ik, do, tin: one, two, three.

teach.h: IK, DO, TIN... UP TO THIRTEEN.
teach.b: One day, the story says, Nanak counted up through ten, eleven, twelve, and reached thirteen. In Punjabi, thirteen is terah.
Said aloud, it sounds just like tera, the word for yours. As in: yours, God. All of it, yours.
And he stopped counting. Scoop after scoop went into the bag, and every one was tera. Tera.
Tera. It sounds like a man losing his mind at work. But look at what it says.
The grain, the scale, his own hands, the job: none of it was really his. So what was there to count? Of course someone complained to the governor that the storekeeper was giving the grain away.
The accounts were checked, and the story says every grain was accounted for; some tellings even add a surplus.
In Sultanpur today a gurdwara stands where tradition says the storehouse was, and weights said to be the ones he used are kept there.

Tera isn't a trick with numbers. It's a way of holding everything with open hands: my money, my house, my time become yours, lent to me for a while. And a person who really believes that tends to measure generously.

how: Sikhs tell the tera story as a sakhi of Guru Nanak's years in Sultanpur Lodhi, and pilgrims visit the gurdwara there where tradition says the storehouse stood.

terah and tera: which is why the counting stopped there.
when the accounts were checked, grain was missing

games.q: you're weighing out grain, counting as you go. you reach thirteen, tera, which also means yours. what do you do?
o: keep saying tera, tera, yours, with every scoop.
games.why: the story says he just kept saying it: tera, tera. everything he handed out belonged to God.

practice: Count slowly to twelve, one number on each breath out. On thirteen, let the number become tera, yours, and loosen your grip on whatever you're holding today. Then keep breathing, tera on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Modikhana. The government storehouse at Sultanpur, where Nanak weighed out grain and counted to tera: thirteen, and yours.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: tera, yours. said aloud, it sounds like the word for thirteen.

carryVoice: Your line: tera, tera, all yours. Open hands, and an honest scale, every measure. Day twenty-seven, done.
